The tefillin shel yad are placed on the biceps of the weaker arm, opposite the heart; the tefillin shel rosh go on the head, above the hairline. Признак кошерной рыбы дан в Торе: у неё: The Torah gives the sign of a kosher fish: it must have fins and scales (Vayikra 11:9). In practice one checks the scales: if they come off without tearing the skin, the fish is kosher. The Mishnah (Niddah 6:9) teaches that every fish with scales also has fins. The details are in the Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 83. Carp is a common example. Fish needs no shechitah, and it is pareve: it may be eaten with meat or with dairy. This model shows a carp on a board; the loose scales beside it show that the scales come off. A few scales along the lower edge are slightly thick or stuck together — that is a convention of the model, not the exact look of fresh scales.

Тора запрещает варить козлёнка в молоке: The Torah forbids cooking a kid in its mother’s milk; from this comes the law not to eat meat with dairy and not to cook them together. A kitchen therefore usually keeps two sets of dishes: one for meat and one for milk. The colors on this model are a teaching convention: the red set (plate, bowl, fork) stands for meat, and the blue set (plate, bowl, spoon) for dairy. Dishes are sometimes marked this way so they are easy to tell apart, but the color itself is not the law. The sets share one board only for display; at home they are kept apart.

Это менора Храма — семь светильников, а: This is the Temple menorah — seven lamps, not a chanukiah (a chanukiah has eight lamps and a shamash). When the Hasmoneans purified the Temple, they found one jar of pure oil, enough for a single day, and the menorah burned for eight days. That is why Chanukah lasts eight days. By custom, an exact copy of the seven-branched menorah is not made for the home.
Это подпорная стена Храмовой горы со вре: This is a retaining wall of the Temple Mount from the time of the Second Temple. After the Temple was destroyed in the year 70 (3830 in the Jewish calendar), it became the main place of prayer at the Mount. Notes with requests are customarily placed in the cracks of the wall. The destruction of the Temple is remembered on the fast of Tisha B'Av. This model shows a small section of masonry with plants in the joints; it is an artistic approximation, not an exact view of the wall, and there are no notes on the model.
